content: Load balancing distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server bears too much demand. It improves availability, fault tolerance, and horizontal scalability. Load balancers operate at Layer 4 (transport) or Layer 7 (application) of the OSI model. Layer 4 load balancers route based on IP and TCP/UDP data; Layer 7 load balancers can inspect HTTP headers, cookies, and request content to make smarter routing decisions. Common algorithms include Round Robin (requests distributed sequentially), Weighted Round Robin (servers assigned weights based on capacity), Least Connections (routes to server with fewest active connections), IP Hash (same client IP always routes to same server for session stickiness), and Random with Two Choices (picks two random servers and routes to the least loaded). Health checks periodically probe backend servers; unhealthy servers are removed from the pool automatically. Popular solutions include HAProxy, NGINX, AWS Elastic Load Balancer (ALB/NLB), and Cloudflare Load Balancing.

Session stickiness (also called sticky sessions or session persistence) ensures that a user's requests are consistently routed to the same backend server during a session. This is needed when session state is stored locally on a server rather than in a shared cache. Sticky sessions can be implemented via IP hashing or cookie-based methods where the load balancer inserts a cookie identifying the target server. Downsides include uneven load distribution and failure handling complexity: if the sticky server goes down, the user loses their session unless sessions are replicated. Best practice is to avoid stickiness entirely by externalizing session state to a shared store like Redis.

topic: Load Balancing - Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB)
content: GSLB distributes traffic across data centers in different geographic regions. It uses DNS-based routing (GeoDNS) or Anycast to direct users to the nearest or healthiest data center. GSLB solves latency, disaster recovery, and compliance (data residency) challenges. When a data center fails, GSLB automatically redirects DNS responses to a healthy region. TTL tuning is critical: short TTLs (30–60s) enable faster failover but increase DNS query load. Implementations include AWS Route 53 Latency-Based Routing, Cloudflare Load Balancing, and Akamai GTM.

Caching stores copies of frequently accessed data in a fast-access storage layer to reduce latency and backend load. Cache hit means the data is found in cache; cache miss means the system must fetch from the source. Key metrics: hit rate (hits / total requests), miss rate, and eviction rate. Cache eviction policies determine what gets removed when cache is full: LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the least recently accessed item, LFU (Least Frequently Used) evicts items with lowest access frequency, FIFO (First In First Out) evicts oldest items, and TTL-based expiry removes items after a set time. Cache invalidation is one of the hardest problems: stale data must be detected and refreshed. Strategies include write-through (cache and DB updated together), write-behind (cache updated first, DB updated asynchronously), and cache-aside (application manages cache explicitly).

Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as cache, message broker, and database. It supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, and geospatial indexes. Redis Cluster provides horizontal sharding across 16384 hash slots with automatic rebalancing. Redis Sentinel provides high availability with automatic failover for master-replica setups. Persistence options: RDB (point-in-time snapshots) and AOF (append-only log of every write operation). Eviction policies include allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-ttl, noeviction. Use cases: session storage, leaderboards (sorted sets), rate limiting (sliding window counters), pub/sub messaging, distributed locks (Redlock algorithm), and caching database query results.

A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers that cache and deliver static and dynamic content from edge nodes close to end users. CDNs reduce latency by serving content from the nearest Point of Presence (PoP), reduce origin server load, and improve availability. Cache-Control and Expires headers control CDN caching behavior. Techniques include cache purging (invalidating specific URLs), cache warming (pre-populating CDN before launch), and stale-while-revalidate (serving stale content while fetching fresh). CDNs also provide DDoS protection, TLS termination, and Web Application Firewall (WAF). Major providers: Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, AWS CloudFront, and Google Cloud CDN. Dynamic content caching uses ESI (Edge Side Includes) or Vary headers to cache personalized content.

Multi-level caching (L1/L2/L3) follows the memory hierarchy model applied to distributed systems. L1 cache: in-process application-level cache (e.g., a HashMap or Guava Cache in the application JVM). Fastest access (~nanoseconds), small capacity, not shared across instances. L2 cache: shared distributed cache like Redis or Memcached. Shared across all application instances, millisecond latency, larger capacity. L3 cache: CDN or reverse proxy cache (NGINX, Varnish). Closest to the user for static assets. Data flows: on a cache miss, fall through each layer until the DB is hit, then populate all cache layers on return. Invalidation must propagate through all layers to avoid stale data.

SQL (relational) databases store data in tables with predefined schemas enforced by ACID transactions. Ideal for complex queries, joins, and strong consistency requirements. Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server. NoSQL databases sacrifice some ACID guarantees for flexibility, horizontal scalability, and schema-less storage. Types include: Document stores (MongoDB, Couchbase) storing JSON-like documents, Key-Value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) for simple lookups, Wide-Column stores (Cassandra, HBase) for time-series and analytical workloads, and Graph databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) for relationship-heavy data. CAP theorem governs trade-offs: you can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. SQL DBs prioritize CA; most NoSQL DBs prioritize AP or CP.

Sharding (horizontal partitioning) splits a database into smaller pieces called shards, each holding a subset of data. Sharding enables horizontal scaling beyond the limits of a single machine. Sharding strategies: Range-based sharding (rows partitioned by value ranges, e.g., user IDs 1–1M on shard 1), Hash-based sharding (shard determined by hash(key) % N, distributes evenly but makes range queries harder), and Directory-based sharding (a lookup table maps keys to shards). Challenges: Cross-shard joins are expensive or impossible; rebalancing shards when adding/removing nodes causes data movement; hot shards (some shards receive disproportionately more traffic) require consistent hashing or virtual nodes. Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping when nodes are added or removed by distributing nodes on a ring.

Database replication copies data from a primary (master) to one or more replicas (slaves/secondaries). Purposes: fault tolerance, read scalability, and geographic distribution. Synchronous replication: primary waits for replica acknowledgment before confirming writes. Guarantees no data loss but increases write latency. Used in PostgreSQL synchronous commit. Asynchronous replication: primary does not wait, replicas may lag behind. Higher write throughput but risk of data loss on failover. Replication lag is the delay between a write on primary and its visibility on replica. Multi-master replication allows writes on multiple nodes; conflict resolution (last-write-wins, CRDTs) is needed. Semi-synchronous replication waits for at least one replica before confirming (MySQL semi-sync).

Database indexes speed up query performance by providing fast lookup paths instead of full table scans. B-tree indexes (default in most SQL DBs) support equality, range, and sort operations efficiently. Hash indexes support only exact equality lookups and are faster for those cases. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) supports full-text search and array containment queries. BRIN (Block Range Index) is efficient for large append-only tables with naturally ordered data (e.g., time-series). Composite indexes cover multiple columns; the order matters - queries must use a left-prefix of the index. Covering indexes include all columns needed by a query, avoiding table access entirely. Partial indexes only index rows meeting a condition, reducing index size. Index bloat occurs when deleted rows are not reclaimed; VACUUM in PostgreSQL reclaims space. Over-indexing degrades write performance since every write must update all indexes.

ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability - the four properties that guarantee reliable database transactions. Atomicity: all operations in a transaction succeed or all are rolled back; no partial state. Consistency: a transaction brings the database from one valid state to another, enforcing constraints and rules. Isolation: concurrent transactions execute as if they were sequential; isolation levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) control how transactions interact. Serializable is the strictest, preventing phantoms and anomalies. Durability: committed transactions survive system failures, ensured by write-ahead logging (WAL). WAL writes changes to a log before applying them to disk; on recovery, the log is replayed.

Connection pooling maintains a pool of reusable database connections to avoid the overhead of establishing a new connection per request (TCP handshake + authentication). A pool manager hands out connections from the pool and returns them after use. Pool size should be tuned: too few connections cause request queuing, too many overwhelm the database. Rule of thumb for PostgreSQL: pool_size = (num_cores * 2) + num_disk_spindles. PgBouncer is a lightweight PostgreSQL connection pooler supporting session, transaction, and statement pooling modes. Transaction pooling is most efficient: a connection is only held for the duration of a transaction. HikariCP is the de facto connection pool for Java applications, renowned for its low overhead.

Message queues enable asynchronous communication between services by decoupling producers and consumers. Producers publish messages to a queue; consumers pull messages at their own pace, enabling backpressure handling and workload leveling. Point-to-point queues (e.g., RabbitMQ, AWS SQS) deliver each message to exactly one consumer. Publish-subscribe systems (e.g., Kafka, Google Pub/Sub) broadcast messages to all subscribed consumers. Key concepts: message acknowledgment (consumer confirms processing), dead-letter queues (messages that fail processing land here for inspection), visibility timeout (message hidden from other consumers while being processed), and message ordering (FIFO queues preserve order at the cost of reduced throughput).

Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant, durable log-based messaging. Core concepts: Topics (logical channels), Partitions (each topic split into ordered, immutable logs), Producers (write to partitions), Consumers (read from partitions by tracking offsets), Consumer Groups (each partition is consumed by exactly one member per group, enabling parallel consumption). Brokers are Kafka server nodes; a cluster has multiple brokers. Replication: each partition has a leader and N-1 followers; all reads and writes go to the leader; followers replicate asynchronously. ZooKeeper (legacy) or KRaft (Kafka Raft metadata mode, Kafka 3.x+) manages broker metadata. Kafka retention: data is retained by time or size, not by consumer acknowledgment, enabling replay and event sourcing. Kafka Connect streams data between Kafka and external systems; Kafka Streams enables stateful stream processing.

RabbitMQ is a message broker implementing AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol). Core components: Exchanges route messages to queues based on routing keys and bindings. Exchange types: Direct (exact routing key match), Fanout (broadcast to all bound queues), Topic (wildcard pattern matching on routing key), Headers (match on message headers). Queues hold messages until consumed. Messages are persisted to disk (durable queues) or stored in memory (transient). Consumer acknowledgments: auto-ack (messages deleted on delivery), manual-ack (consumer explicitly acknowledges). Dead-letter exchanges handle unroutable or expired messages. RabbitMQ clustering partitions queues across nodes; Quorum Queues (Raft-based replication) provide high availability without classic mirrored queues. Shovel and Federation plugins enable cross-cluster message routing.

Microservices architecture structures an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each owning its domain and data. Services communicate via APIs (REST, gRPC) or asynchronous messaging. Principles: Single Responsibility (each service does one thing well), Loose Coupling (minimal inter-service dependencies), High Cohesion (related functionality co-located), Data Isolation (each service owns its database, no shared DB). Advantages: independent scaling, independent deployment, polyglot persistence and language freedom, fault isolation. Challenges: network latency, distributed transactions, service discovery, observability complexity, and data consistency across services. Conway's Law states system architecture mirrors organizational communication structure, making team topology important for microservice design.

A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer handling service-to-service communication, providing traffic management, security, and observability without application code changes. Implemented as sidecar proxies (e.g., Envoy) deployed alongside each service instance. Features: mutual TLS (mTLS) for service authentication and encryption, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts, rate limiting, traffic shaping (A/B testing, canary deployments), distributed tracing, and metrics collection. Control planes: Istio (comprehensive, complex), Linkerd (lightweight, opinionated), Consul Connect (HashiCorp ecosystem). Service meshes add latency overhead (2–10ms per hop) due to the extra proxy hop; evaluate if the operational benefit justifies this cost.

An API Gateway is a single entry point for all client requests in a microservices system. It handles cross-cutting concerns including: authentication and authorization (JWT validation, OAuth2), rate limiting and throttling, request routing and load balancing, SSL termination, request/response transformation (protocol translation, payload modification), caching of responses, and API composition (aggregating multiple microservice calls into one response). Benefits: client simplification (single endpoint instead of many), centralized security, and reduced coupling. Patterns: Backend for Frontend (BFF) creates tailored APIs per client type (mobile, web, third-party). Popular solutions: AWS API Gateway, Kong, NGINX, Traefik, Apigee, and Tyk. Ensure the gateway does not become a monolith of business logic.

The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures in distributed systems by detecting repeated failures and temporarily stopping requests to a struggling service. States: Closed (normal operation, requests pass through, failure count tracked), Open (failures exceeded threshold, requests fail immediately without attempting the downstream call), Half-Open (after a timeout, limited requests are allowed through to test recovery). Parameters: failure threshold (e.g., 5 failures in 10 seconds opens the circuit), timeout duration (time the circuit stays open), and success threshold (how many successes in half-open state close the circuit). Fallbacks on open circuit include cached data, default responses, or graceful degradation. Implementations: Netflix Hystrix (deprecated), Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), Istio circuit breaking at the mesh level.

The Saga pattern manages distributed transactions across multiple microservices without a two-phase commit (2PC) by breaking them into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating transaction for rollback. Two implementation styles: Choreography (each service listens for events and triggers the next step, no central coordinator; suitable for simple flows but hard to debug) and Orchestration (a central saga orchestrator sends commands to services and handles failures; easier to reason about for complex flows). Compensating transactions must be idempotent. Example: order service creates order, payment service charges card, inventory service reserves stock. If inventory fails, saga executes compensating transactions to reverse payment and cancel order. Sagas provide eventual consistency, not ACID; ACD (Atomicity via compensations, Consistency eventual, Durability per local transaction) is the achievable model.

Event Sourcing stores the state of a system as an ordered, immutable log of events rather than the current state snapshot. The current state is derived by replaying events. Benefits: complete audit trail, temporal queries (reconstruct state at any point in time), event replay for debugging, and natural integration with CQRS. Challenges: event schema evolution (events are immutable; versioning requires upcasters or new event types), eventually consistent read models, snapshot optimization (periodic snapshots prevent replaying entire event log), and increased storage. Event stores: EventStoreDB, Axon, Kafka (as a durable log). Anti-pattern: using event sourcing for all data - use it only where auditability and temporal queries add value.

CQRS separates the read model (queries) from the write model (commands) into distinct models and often separate data stores. The write side handles commands that mutate state and emits events. The read side maintains denormalized, query-optimized projections updated by event handlers. Benefits: each model can be independently optimized (write side for consistency, read side for query performance and schema), independent scaling of read and write workloads, and simpler models on each side. Challenges: eventual consistency between write and read models (read model may lag), increased complexity in synchronization, and maintaining multiple data stores. CQRS pairs naturally with Event Sourcing: events generated by the write side are projected into read model stores (Elasticsearch, Redis, specialized SQL views).

Rate limiting controls the rate of requests a client can make to protect APIs from abuse and overload. Algorithms: Token Bucket (tokens added at a fixed rate to a bucket of max capacity; each request consumes one token; bursts allowed up to bucket capacity; most common in practice), Leaky Bucket (requests enter a queue and are processed at a fixed rate; smooth output but drops bursts), Fixed Window Counter (count requests per fixed time window; allows burst at window boundary), Sliding Window Log (log every request timestamp; count requests in the last N seconds for each request; accurate but memory-intensive), Sliding Window Counter (approximation combining fixed window counts at window boundaries; memory-efficient and accurate). Distributed rate limiting uses Redis with atomic Lua scripts or Redis cell module. Headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

Consistent hashing is an algorithm used in distributed systems to distribute data across nodes (cache servers, shards) with minimal redistribution when nodes are added or removed. Nodes and keys are mapped to positions on a conceptual ring (modular hash space). Each key is assigned to the nearest node clockwise on the ring. When a node is added, only the keys between the new node and its predecessor need to move. When a node is removed, only its keys are redistributed to its successor. Virtual nodes (vnodes) improve balance by assigning multiple ring positions per physical node, compensating for uneven key distribution. Used in: Cassandra (partition key hashing to vnodes), Memcached client-side sharding, Amazon Dynamo, and Riak.

Raft is a distributed consensus algorithm that ensures all nodes in a cluster agree on a sequence of values (log entries). It is designed to be more understandable than Paxos. Roles: Leader (handles all client requests, replicates log to followers), Follower (passive, responds to requests from leader or candidate), Candidate (starts election when leader heartbeat times out). Leader Election: followers become candidates and request votes; a candidate wins if it receives votes from a majority. Log Replication: leader appends entries to its log, sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers; entry is committed when a majority acknowledge it. Safety: only candidates with the most up-to-date log can win elections. Used in: etcd (Kubernetes backing store), CockroachDB, TiKV, Consul.

Paxos is a foundational distributed consensus algorithm allowing a network of unreliable nodes to agree on a single value despite failures. Phases: Prepare (proposer sends prepare request with proposal number N to a quorum of acceptors; acceptors promise not to accept lower-numbered proposals), Promise (acceptors respond with highest previously accepted value), Accept (proposer sends accept request with value; acceptors accept if no higher proposal seen), Commit (once a quorum accepts, the value is chosen). Multi-Paxos optimizes by electing a stable leader to skip prepare phase for subsequent proposals. Paxos is notoriously difficult to implement correctly; Raft was designed as a more understandable alternative. Used in: Google Chubby, Google Spanner.

The CAP Theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a response, though it may not be the most recent), and Partition Tolerance (the system continues operating despite network partitions). Since network partitions are unavoidable in real distributed systems, the practical choice is CP (consistency + partition tolerance, e.g., HBase, Zookeeper, Spanner) or AP (availability + partition tolerance, e.g., DynamoDB, Cassandra, CouchDB). PACELC extends CAP: even without partitions, there is a trade-off between latency and consistency. Most modern databases allow configurable consistency levels to tune the trade-off per operation.

Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made to a distributed data item, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. Used in AP systems to maximize availability. Conflict resolution strategies: Last Write Wins (LWW) uses timestamps to pick the latest write (risk of clock skew issues), Vector Clocks track causality between versions (each node maintains a version counter per replica), CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are data structures that can be merged automatically without conflicts (examples: G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set, LWW-Register), and Operational Transformation (used in Google Docs for concurrent editing). Application-level conflict resolution lets the application merge conflicting writes (Amazon shopping cart model). Strong eventual consistency (SEC) systems provide conflict-free convergence using CRDTs.

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for APIs using HTTP methods to operate on resources. Best practices: use nouns for resources (not verbs), nest resources to represent hierarchy (/users/{id}/orders), use HTTP methods semantically (GET read, POST create, PUT full update, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove), return appropriate HTTP status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error), version APIs via URL prefix (/v1/) or header, use pagination with cursor-based (keyset) pagination for large collections, support filtering, sorting, and field selection via query params, use HATEOAS links for discoverability, document with OpenAPI/Swagger, and validate inputs returning clear error payloads.

gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport. Advantages over REST: strongly typed contracts defined in .proto files, binary serialization (smaller payload, faster parsing), HTTP/2 multiplexing (multiple concurrent streams over one connection), native bidirectional streaming, and auto-generated client SDKs in 10+ languages. Four communication patterns: Unary (request-response), Server Streaming (server streams responses), Client Streaming (client streams requests), Bidirectional Streaming. Ideal for: internal microservice-to-microservice communication, real-time data push, IoT, and mobile-backend communication where bandwidth matters. Limitations: not human-readable (requires tooling), limited browser support (gRPC-Web adapter required), and harder to debug than REST.

GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs enabling clients to request exactly the data they need. Core concepts: Schema (strongly typed, defines types, queries, mutations, subscriptions), Resolvers (functions that fetch data for each field), Queries (read data), Mutations (write data), Subscriptions (real-time updates via WebSockets). Advantages: no over-fetching or under-fetching, single endpoint, self-documenting schema, strong typing, and client-driven data shapes. Challenges: N+1 problem (each nested field resolver triggers a DB query; solved with DataLoader batching), complex query abuse (clients can request deeply nested expensive queries; mitigated with query depth limiting, query complexity analysis, and persisted queries), and caching is harder than REST (responses not cacheable by URL alone; use persisted query IDs or CDN with cache hints).

Design of a URL shortener like bit.ly. Requirements: given a long URL, generate a short unique code; redirect short URL to original. Scale assumptions: 100M URLs created/day (write-heavy), 10B redirects/day (read-heavy, ~100:1 read:write ratio). Short code generation: encode a 64-bit auto-increment ID to base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) yields 7-character codes (62^7 = 3.5 trillion unique codes). Alternatively use MD5/SHA1 of URL and take first 7 characters (collision risk requires handling). Storage: each URL mapping ~100 bytes; 100M/day * 365 * 5 years = 182TB for 5 years. Cache: 20% of URLs account for 80% of traffic (Pareto); cache hot URLs in Redis. Redirect: HTTP 301 (permanent, browser caches, reduces server load) vs 302 (temporary, traffic tracked every time, preferred for analytics). DB schema: {id, short_code, long_url, created_at, expires_at, user_id}. Read path: short_code -> Redis cache -> DB -> HTTP redirect. Custom aliases require unique constraint on short_code.

Designing a social media news feed at Twitter scale. Core challenge: fan-out on write vs fan-out on read. Fan-out on write (push): when a user tweets, precompute and push the tweet into all followers' feed caches. Low read latency (feed is precomputed). Problem: celebrities with 100M followers cause massive write amplification. Fan-out on read (pull): feed is computed at read time by fetching tweets from all followed accounts and merging. Simple writes, but expensive reads scale with number of follows. Hybrid approach (Twitter's actual model): fan-out on write for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities (>X followers). Tweet storage: Cassandra for distributed write-heavy workload, MySQL for user metadata. Timeline aggregation: merge sort K sorted tweet streams by timestamp. Cache: Redis sorted sets per user storing tweet IDs (not full tweet data) to keep cache small; fetch tweet content from a separate tweet cache.

Designing a distributed file storage system like Google Drive or S3. Components: Metadata service (stores file metadata: name, size, owner, version, block list in a relational DB with strong consistency), Block/Chunk storage (files split into fixed-size chunks, e.g., 64MB, each stored with replication across data nodes), Sync client (detects file changes via file watchers, breaks files into chunks, uploads only changed chunks using delta sync), and API servers (handle client requests). Chunking enables: deduplication (identical chunks stored once, identified by content hash), parallel uploads (chunks uploaded concurrently), and efficient sync (only modified chunks transferred). Metadata DB tracks: {file_id, name, version, chunk_list, owner}. Replication: each chunk replicated 3x across different availability zones. Consistency: version vectors or timestamps detect conflicts. Long tail latency mitigation: hedge requests (send same chunk request to multiple replicas, use first response).

Designing a distributed rate limiter. Requirements: limit API calls per user per time window, return 429 Too Many Requests when exceeded, work across multiple API server instances. Architecture: centralized counter in Redis using atomic operations. Token bucket with Redis: use a sorted set storing request timestamps; on each request, remove timestamps older than the window, count remaining, compare to limit, add current timestamp atomically using a Lua script. Sliding window counter with Redis: store two counters (current window and previous window), approximate current rate as prev_count * (1 - elapsed/window) + curr_count. Sticky sessions route users to the same rate-limiter shard to avoid distributed coordination, but requires consistent hashing on user ID. Rules engine: rate limit rules stored in config files or DB (e.g., 100 requests/minute for free tier, 1000/minute for premium). Middleware layer: rate limiter implemented as middleware before routing to business logic.

Designing a distributed cache system like Memcached or Redis at scale. Requirements: sub-millisecond reads, horizontal scalability, high availability. Architecture: consistent hashing ring distributes keys across cache nodes. Client library routes requests to appropriate node based on key hash. Replication: each cache node has a primary and one or more replicas for HA. On node failure, consistent hashing minimizes cache misses (only keys from failed node re-route to neighbor). Cache coherence challenge: multiple nodes caching same data from DB may have stale copies; solutions include TTL-based expiry, event-driven invalidation (DB triggers invalidation event to all cache nodes), and pub/sub invalidation channels. Thundering herd (cache stampede): when a popular key expires, many requests simultaneously miss and hit the DB. Mitigations: probabilistic early expiration, mutex-based cache-aside (one request locks key and fetches, others wait), and background refresh before expiry.

Designing a search autocomplete (typeahead) system. Requirements: return top-k suggestions for a query prefix, sub-100ms latency, updated with trending searches daily. Trie data structure: prefix tree mapping characters to nodes; each node stores top-k completions for that prefix. Trie construction: process historical search logs, aggregate query frequencies, build trie with top-k at each node. Scale challenge: trie is too large for a single server (~GB). Solutions: shard trie by first character(s), cache hot prefix results in Redis (first 2-3 characters cover 90% of queries). Update strategy: rebuild trie weekly from Hadoop/Spark batch job, deploy as immutable snapshots. Real-time trending: maintain a separate stream-based counter (Kafka + Flink) for recent N hours, blend with historical trie rankings using weighted score. Serving: dedicated autocomplete service with trie in memory, load-balanced, Redis L2 cache for frequent prefixes. API: GET /autocomplete?q={prefix}&lang={lang}&limit={k}.

Designing a push notification system. Channels: push notifications (iOS APNs, Android FCM), SMS (Twilio, SNS), email (SendGrid, SES), in-app notifications. Architecture: Notification API receives notification request, validates and stores in DB. Worker pulls from queue (Kafka/SQS) and routes to appropriate channel provider. Retry logic: exponential backoff with dead-letter queue for failed deliveries. Device token management: store device tokens per user, refresh stale tokens on delivery failure. Priority queues: separate queues for critical (OTP, security alerts) vs marketing notifications. Fanout for group notifications: one event produces N notifications (one per recipient); push fan-out work to workers to handle large groups asynchronously. Analytics: track delivery, open, and click events via callback webhooks from channel providers. Rate limiting: prevent notification spam per user. Preferences: user preference service stores channel opt-ins and quiet hours.

topic: System Design - Ride Sharing Location Service
content: Designing a real-time location service for ride-sharing (Uber/Lyft). Challenges: ingest millions of GPS updates per minute from driver apps, match riders to nearby drivers efficiently, and broadcast location updates to rider apps. Location update pipeline: driver app sends GPS coordinates every 4 seconds, WebSocket or gRPC streaming to location service, published to Kafka for durable processing. Geospatial indexing: drivers partitioned by geographic cells using S2 geometry library (Google) or H3 (Uber). Cell hierarchy allows querying at different resolutions. Redis GEOADD stores driver locations; GEORADIUS or GEORADIUSBYMEMBER finds drivers within N km. Matching: find available drivers in expanding radius rings from rider location, rank by ETA using road network distance (not Euclidean). Supply/demand heatmaps: aggregate driver density per cell in real-time using Flink for surge pricing calculation. Historical location data stored in Cassandra (time-series, high write throughput).

Generating globally unique IDs at scale. Requirements: unique across all nodes, roughly time-sortable, compact, not sequential (to prevent enumeration), high throughput. Options: UUID v4 (128-bit random, globally unique, no coordination required, not sortable, 36 chars), Twitter Snowflake (64-bit: 41 bits timestamp + 10 bits machine ID + 12 bits sequence; ~4096 IDs/ms per machine, sortable, compact), ULIDv (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier: 26 char base32, 48-bit timestamp + 80-bit random, sortable), Database auto-increment (not scalable across shards), and Ticket Server (centralized ID service; single point of failure unless replicated with odd/even IDs per node). Snowflake architecture: each service instance has a unique machine ID assigned at startup via ZooKeeper or similar; clock skew handling requires rejecting requests if system clock goes backward.

Distributed locking coordinates access to shared resources across multiple processes or servers. Redis-based locking (Redlock algorithm): SET key value NX PX timeout where NX=not exists, PX=millisecond expiry. Acquire lock by setting key; release by deleting key (only if value matches, verified with Lua script to prevent deleting another process's lock). Redlock acquires locks on N/2+1 of N independent Redis nodes; majority ensures lock even if some nodes fail. Lease-based locking: locks have TTL; holders must renew (heartbeat) before expiry; failure to renew releases lock. Use cases: preventing double-processing in distributed systems, coordinating leader election, and throttling access to external APIs. ZooKeeper-based locking: ephemeral sequential znodes; lowest-numbered node holds lock; others watch the next lower node, enabling fair FIFO locking. Considerations: clock skew, long GC pauses invalidating lock assumptions, and fencing tokens for safety.

Observability is the ability to understand the internal state of a system from its external outputs. Three pillars: Metrics (aggregated numerical measurements over time: counters, gauges, histograms, percentiles; examples: request rate, latency p99, error rate, CPU usage), Logs (structured records of discrete events with context: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, user_id, message; use structured JSON logs, centralize in ELK stack or Loki), Distributed Tracing (tracks a request as it flows through multiple services; each request gets a trace_id; each service call creates a span with start/end time and metadata; visualized as flame graphs or Gantt charts; tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray, OpenTelemetry). SLIs (Service Level Indicators): measurable metrics (availability, latency). SLOs (Service Level Objectives): targets (99.9% uptime). SLAs (Service Level Agreements): contractual commitments. Error budgets: 1 - SLO; time you can spend on risk before violating SLO.

Prometheus is an open-source monitoring and alerting system using a pull-based model: it scrapes metrics from /metrics endpoints of instrumented services at regular intervals. Data model: multidimensional time series identified by metric name and key-value labels. PromQL is the query language for aggregation and alerting. Metric types: Counter (monotonically increasing, e.g., total requests), Gauge (current value, e.g., active connections), Histogram (bucketed observations for latency distribution, enables Apdex and percentile calculation), Summary (similar to histogram but computes quantiles client-side). Alertmanager routes alerts to PagerDuty, Slack, email based on severity and routing rules. Alert silencing and inhibition prevent alert storms. Grafana visualizes Prometheus data in dashboards with panels, variables, and annotations. Recording rules precompute expensive PromQL expressions. Long-term storage: Thanos or Cortex extend Prometheus with global query view and durable object storage.

Service discovery allows services to find each other dynamically without hardcoded IP addresses. Client-side discovery: client queries a service registry (Consul, Eureka, Zookeeper), gets list of instances, and load-balances itself (Netflix Ribbon pattern). Server-side discovery: client makes request to a router/load balancer which queries the registry and forwards (AWS ELB + Cloud Map). Service registries: Consul (distributed, strongly consistent, supports health checks, DNS and HTTP API), Etcd (key-value store with watch capabilities), Eureka (Netflix OSS, AP, self-preservation mode). Registration: self-registration (service registers itself on startup and deregisters on shutdown), third-party registration (orchestrator like Kubernetes registers services via endpoints). Kubernetes uses kube-proxy and CoreDNS: every Service gets a stable DNS name (my-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local) that resolves to its ClusterIP, which routes to healthy pod endpoints.

Docker containers package applications with their dependencies into isolated, portable units. Images are layered filesystems built from Dockerfiles; layers are cached for efficient builds. Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestration platform. Core objects: Pod (smallest deployable unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage), Deployment (desired state for a set of replicated pods, handles rolling updates and rollbacks), Service (stable network endpoint for a set of pods via label selectors), Ingress (HTTP/HTTPS routing from outside the cluster to services), ConfigMap (non-secret configuration), Secret (sensitive data stored base64-encoded, often backed by Vault), PersistentVolume (external storage attached to pods). Scheduling: kube-scheduler places pods on nodes based on resource requests/limits, affinity rules, and taints/tolerations. Autoscaling: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) scales pod replicas based on CPU/memory or custom metrics; VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) adjusts resource requests; Cluster Autoscaler adds/removes nodes.

Continuous Integration (CI) automatically builds and tests code on every commit to detect integration issues early. Continuous Delivery (CD) ensures code is always in a deployable state; Continuous Deployment automatically deploys every passed build to production. CI pipeline stages: code commit trigger, dependency install, unit tests, integration tests, static analysis (linting, SAST), build artifact (Docker image), push to registry, and notify. CD pipeline stages: pull artifact, deploy to staging, run smoke/E2E tests, deploy to production (gated by approval or auto on success). Deployment strategies: Rolling (replace pods one by one), Blue-Green (two identical environments, switch traffic), Canary (route small % to new version, monitor, gradually increase), Feature Flags (deploy code but toggle features per user segment). Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, ArgoCD (GitOps for K8s), Spinnaker.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) manages and provisions infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes. Benefits: version control, reproducibility, code review for infrastructure changes, and automated provisioning. Terraform (HashiCorp): declarative HCL language, provider-agnostic (AWS, GCP, Azure, K8s), state file tracks real infrastructure, plan shows diff before apply, modules enable reuse. AWS CloudFormation: AWS-native, JSON/YAML templates, stacks manage lifecycle. Pulumi: imperative IaC using general-purpose languages (Python, TypeScript). Ansible: agentless configuration management using SSH and YAML playbooks, idempotent tasks. Chef/Puppet: agent-based configuration management with centralized policy server. GitOps pattern: desired infrastructure state stored in Git; operators (ArgoCD, Flux) continuously reconcile actual state to match.

Authentication (AuthN) verifies identity (who are you?); Authorization (AuthZ) verifies permissions (what can you do?). Authentication methods: username/password (hash with bcrypt, Argon2; never store plaintext), OAuth 2.0 (delegated authorization framework; access tokens grant scoped access to resources; flows: Authorization Code with PKCE for web/mobile, Client Credentials for machine-to-machine), OpenID Connect (identity layer on OAuth 2.0; ID token as JWT proves identity), SAML 2.0 (XML-based SSO for enterprise), FIDO2/WebAuthn (phishing-resistant passwordless using device biometrics/hardware keys), and MFA (TOTP apps like Google Authenticator, SMS OTP, hardware tokens). JWT (JSON Web Token): header.payload.signature; signed but not encrypted by default (use JWE for encryption); stateless; validate signature and expiry on every request. Authorization models: RBAC (Role-Based: permissions assigned to roles assigned to users), ABAC (Attribute-Based: policies on user/resource/environment attributes), ReBAC (Relationship-Based: Google Zanzibar model, permissions based on graph relationships).

Zero Trust is a security model operating on the principle 'never trust, always verify' - no implicit trust based on network location (inside/outside the perimeter). Core tenets: verify explicitly (authenticate and authorize every request with all available signals: identity, device health, location, service), use least privilege access (just-in-time, just-enough-access), and assume breach (minimize blast radius, segment access, detect anomalies). Implementation: strong identity for users (MFA, device compliance) and workloads (mutual TLS, service accounts), micro-segmentation of networks (prevent lateral movement), continuous monitoring and analytics (behavioral baselines, anomaly detection), and data classification with encryption. Tools: BeyondCorp (Google's Zero Trust model), Cloudflare Access, Zscaler ZPA, HashiCorp Vault (secrets management), and OPA (Open Policy Agent) for fine-grained authorization.

Encryption at rest: AES-256-GCM encrypts data stored on disk. Key management is critical: use HSMs (Hardware Security Modules) or cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) to store and rotate encryption keys; never hardcode keys. Encryption in transit: TLS 1.3 (deprecated TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2 where possible); enforce HSTS for web services; use mTLS for service-to-service communication. Database encryption: TDE (Transparent Data Encryption) encrypts database files at the storage level. Application-level encryption: encrypt sensitive fields (PII, payment data) before storing; preserves ability to query specific fields while protecting others. Hashing: one-way transformation for passwords (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt with salt) and integrity verification (SHA-256, SHA-3). HMAC for message authentication codes. Key rotation: regular rotation of cryptographic keys; design systems to support rotation without downtime using key versioning.

DNS (Domain Name System) is the hierarchical distributed naming system translating domain names to IP addresses. Resolution process: client queries local resolver cache, then recursive resolver (ISP or public like 8.8.8.8), which queries root nameservers, TLD nameservers (.com, .org), then authoritative nameservers for the domain. TTL determines cache duration. Record types: A (IPv4 address), AAAA (IPv6 address), CNAME (alias to another name, cannot be at zone apex), ALIAS/ANAME (CNAME-like at apex), MX (mail exchange), TXT (text, used for SPF, DKIM, domain verification), NS (nameserver delegation), SOA (zone start of authority). DNSSEC adds digital signatures to prevent cache poisoning. DNS-based load balancing: return multiple A records (round-robin DNS). Anycast routing: same IP announced from multiple data centers, BGP routes traffic to nearest PoP.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides reliable, ordered, connection-oriented delivery with congestion control. Three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) establishes connection. Features: retransmission of lost packets, flow control (receiver window), congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit), and in-order delivery. Head-of-line blocking: a lost packet blocks all subsequent packets in the stream until retransmitted. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless, with no guarantees of delivery, order, or duplication prevention. Lower overhead, lower latency. Used for: video streaming, VoIP, DNS (short request-response where retransmit is handled at application level), and gaming. QUIC (HTTP/3): built on UDP, provides TLS 1.3 encryption, streams to prevent head-of-line blocking (packet loss in one stream doesn't block others), and faster connection establishment (0-RTT or 1-RTT vs TCP+TLS 3-RTT).

Real-time communication patterns for server-to-client push. Short Polling: client repeatedly requests data at intervals. Simple but wasteful (empty responses). Long Polling: client makes a request; server holds it open until new data available or timeout, then client immediately reconnects. Reduces empty responses but still one request per update. Server-Sent Events (SSE): HTTP-based one-way stream from server to client. Automatic reconnection, event IDs for resumption. Good for live feeds, dashboards. Works over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. WebSockets: full-duplex persistent connection over a single TCP connection. HTTP upgrade handshake (Upgrade: websocket header). Enables low-latency bidirectional messaging. Used for: chat, collaborative editing, multiplayer games, trading platforms. WebSocket challenges: sticky load balancing required (or use a pub/sub layer like Redis to broadcast across stateless server instances), connection management at scale (10K+ concurrent connections per server with async I/O). Socket.IO wraps WebSockets with fallback and room abstractions.

topic: Data Pipelines - Batch vs Stream Processing
content: Batch processing handles large volumes of data collected over a period, processed together. High throughput, higher latency (minutes to hours). Tools: Apache Spark, Apache Hadoop MapReduce, AWS Glue. Stream processing handles data in real-time or near-real-time as it arrives, record by record or in micro-batches. Low latency (milliseconds to seconds). Tools: Apache Flink (stateful stream processing, exactly-once semantics, event time processing, watermarks for out-of-order events), Apache Spark Streaming, Apache Storm, AWS Kinesis Data Analytics. Lambda architecture combines batch (accurate, historical) and speed (real-time, approximate) layers with a serving layer merging results. Kappa architecture uses only a streaming layer, replaying historical data from Kafka when needed. Event time vs processing time: event time is when the event occurred; processing time is when it was processed. Watermarks track progress of event time to handle late-arriving data.

ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) extracts data from sources, transforms it in a staging area, then loads the result into the data warehouse. Transformation happens before loading; requires significant compute outside the warehouse. Traditional approach for on-premise data warehouses with limited storage. ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the data warehouse first, then transforms it using the warehouse's compute (SQL). Enabled by cloud data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) with cheap storage and massive parallel processing. Advantages: raw data preserved for re-transformation, faster time-to-value, leverages warehouse scalability. Data lineage tracks data provenance through transformation steps. Tools: dbt (data build tool) - SQL-based ELT transformations with dependency management, testing, and documentation. Airbyte, Fivetran, Stitch for managed ELT connectors. Apache Airflow for workflow orchestration.

Disaster Recovery (DR) is the process of restoring IT systems after a disaster. Key metrics: RTO (Recovery Time Objective - maximum acceptable downtime), RPO (Recovery Point Objective - maximum acceptable data loss window). DR strategies by cost/complexity: Backup and Restore (cheapest, highest RTO/RPO; restore from backup on new infrastructure; hours-days recovery), Pilot Light (minimal running infrastructure in DR region, core DB replicating; warm up rest of stack on failover; minutes-hours RTO), Warm Standby (scaled-down but fully functional duplicate environment running; fast failover but some capacity increase needed), Active-Active (multi-region active traffic; near-zero RTO/RPO; most expensive). Runbook automation: DR procedures documented and automated (Terraform + scripts) to reduce human error under stress. Regular DR drills (chaos engineering): Netflix Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances to verify resilience. GameDays simulate failure scenarios with full incident response.

Chaos Engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into a system to proactively identify weaknesses before they cause outages. Principles: define steady state (measurable hypothesis of normal behavior), hypothesize that steady state will continue through chaos, inject realistic variables (server crashes, network latency, disk full, dependency failures), and verify or disprove the hypothesis. Netflix pioneered chaos engineering with Chaos Monkey (terminates random EC2 instances in production). Gremlin and Chaos Toolkit are managed chaos platforms. Failure modes to test: instance termination, AZ failure, network latency injection, packet loss, CPU stress, memory pressure, dependency timeouts, and DNS failures. Blast radius: start small (non-production, canary traffic), expand as confidence grows. Game Days: structured chaos experiments with the full team present to test incident response. Chaos engineering should be a continuous practice, not a one-time event.

topic: Scalability Patterns - Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
content: Vertical scaling (scaling up) adds more resources to an existing machine (more CPU, RAM, faster storage). Simple to implement, no application changes required, but has physical hardware limits, single point of failure, and downtime during scaling. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more machines to distribute the workload. Requires stateless application design (no local state) or shared state externalization (sessions to Redis, files to S3). Enables near-unlimited scale and higher fault tolerance. Enables geographic distribution. Challenges: distributed systems complexity, data partitioning, and network overhead. Auto-scaling: automatically add/remove instances based on metrics (CPU, request rate, queue depth). AWS Auto Scaling Groups, Kubernetes HPA/KEDA. Scaling triggers: reactive (scale when metric exceeds threshold), predictive (scale based on scheduled patterns), and proactive (scale ahead of known events like marketing campaigns).

Read replicas offload read queries from the primary database, improving read throughput and reducing primary load. Most production workloads are read-heavy (80-95% reads), making read replicas highly effective. The primary handles all writes and replicates to N read replicas asynchronously. Replication lag (typically <100ms) means replicas may serve slightly stale data - acceptable for most use cases (product listings, user profiles) but not for immediately-consistent reads (post-write verification, financial balances). Application routing: ORM-level read/write splitting (e.g., Django DATABASE_ROUTERS, SQLAlchemy), proxy-level splitting (ProxySQL, MaxScale). Read replica auto-scaling: Aurora Auto Scaling and RDS read replica promotion. Cross-region read replicas reduce latency for globally distributed users and serve as DR targets. Avoid query patterns that route too many writes to replicas (e.g., SELECT FOR UPDATE must go to primary).

Asynchronous processing decouples long-running or non-urgent work from the request-response cycle, improving API responsiveness and system resilience. Pattern: API receives request, validates input, enqueues a job, returns 202 Accepted with a job ID. Worker processes job in background. Client polls /jobs/{id}/status or receives webhook/push notification on completion. Use cases: image/video processing, sending emails and notifications, report generation, payment processing, data imports/exports, and ML inference. Task queues: Celery (Python), Sidekiq (Ruby), BullMQ (Node.js), Resque. Broker options: Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS. Worker concurrency and autoscaling: workers scaled by queue depth. Job retry with exponential backoff. Idempotency: jobs designed to be safe to retry without duplicate side effects (use idempotency keys). Priority queues: critical jobs processed before background jobs.

The Bulkhead pattern isolates elements of an application into pools so that if one fails, the others continue to function. Named after ship hull compartmentalization. Implementation: separate thread pools or connection pools per downstream dependency. If service A calls services B and C with a shared thread pool and B is slow, B's slow responses exhaust all threads, preventing calls to C. With bulkheads, B gets its own thread pool (e.g., 10 threads) and C gets its own (10 threads); B's failures don't starve C. Semaphore isolation is a lighter alternative: limit concurrent calls to each dependency using a semaphore. Applied in: HTTP client connection pools per host, database connection pools per service, service instance isolation in K8s via resource limits and namespace quotas. Hystrix implements bulkhead isolation. Combine with circuit breakers for full resilience.

The Strangler Fig pattern incrementally migrates a monolithic system to microservices by gradually replacing specific pieces of functionality with new services while the monolith handles the rest. Named after the fig tree that grows around a host tree until the host dies. Process: deploy a routing facade (API gateway or proxy) in front of the monolith; gradually route specific endpoints to new microservices as they are built; when all functionality is migrated, the monolith is retired. Anti-corruption layer: adapter between old and new systems to translate models. Risk mitigation: never rewrite everything at once; run new and old in parallel and compare outputs before full cutover. Event interception: capture events from the monolith to drive the new service without tight coupling. Successfully used by: Shopify, Netflix, and many enterprises migrating from monoliths.

The Outbox Pattern ensures atomicity between database writes and message publishing in distributed systems. Problem: a service must update the database and publish an event; if the DB update succeeds but the message broker is unavailable, the event is lost, leaving the system in an inconsistent state. Solution: within the same DB transaction, write the business data and write the event to an outbox table. A message relay process (Debezium CDC, or a polling publisher) reads the outbox table and publishes events to the broker, then marks them as sent. Guarantees at-least-once delivery (message relay may retry; consumers must be idempotent). Transactional outbox eliminates dual-write problems without distributed transactions. Debezium uses PostgreSQL/MySQL WAL to stream outbox table changes to Kafka with minimal polling overhead.

The Sidecar pattern deploys a helper component alongside a primary application container in the same pod or host, extending or augmenting the primary's capabilities without modifying it. Common sidecars: Envoy proxy (service mesh, TLS, tracing, retry logic), log shippers (Fluentd, Filebeat collecting logs from shared volume), secret injectors (Vault Agent injecting secrets as files), monitoring agents (Datadog Agent), and security scanners. Benefits: separation of concerns (application focuses on business logic), technology agnosticism (sidecar works regardless of application language), and independent lifecycle (sidecar can be updated without redeploying the application). In Kubernetes: defined as multiple containers in one Pod spec sharing network namespace (localhost communication) and volumes. Istio's sidecar injection automatically adds Envoy to pods via a MutatingWebhookConfiguration.

The Ambassador pattern deploys a helper service that sends network requests on behalf of a consumer, acting as an out-of-process proxy. Similar to sidecar but typically used for handling complex client logic externally. Use cases: adding retry logic and circuit breaking without modifying the client application, offloading TLS and authentication, monitoring and logging outbound requests, and routing requests based on environment (dev vs prod). Difference from sidecar: Ambassador is consumer-specific (client-side) while sidecar can augment either side. Example: Envoy deployed as an ambassador handles all outbound calls from a legacy application that cannot be modified. Linkerd and Consul Connect act as ambassadors in service mesh configurations. In Kubernetes, ambassador containers run in the same pod as the application container but handle all external communication.

The Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) is a translation layer between two subsystems that have different domain models or languages. It prevents a legacy or external system's model from 'leaking' into and corrupting the domain model of the new system. The ACL translates requests and responses between the two models in both directions. Used in: Strangler Fig migrations (translating between monolith and microservice models), third-party integrations (wrapping external APIs in domain-aligned interfaces), and bounded context integration in Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Implementation: Facades that wrap the external API, Adapters that translate data models, and Services that orchestrate the translation. The ACL adds a layer of indirection that allows the external system to change without affecting the internal model, and vice versa.

Domain-Driven Design is an approach to software development where the domain model is the center of development, focusing on complex business logic. Key concepts: Ubiquitous Language (shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts used in code and conversations), Bounded Context (explicit boundary within which a domain model is defined and applicable; different bounded contexts may use different models for the same concept), Entity (object with a unique identity that persists over time), Value Object (immutable object defined by its attributes, no identity), Aggregate (cluster of entities and value objects with a single root entity enforcing invariants; transactions limited to one aggregate), Domain Events (events that capture state changes significant to the domain), Repository (abstraction for accessing aggregates from persistence), and Domain Service (business logic that doesn't belong to an entity or value object).

The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology for building scalable, maintainable SaaS applications. The twelve factors: 1) Codebase (one codebase tracked in version control, many deploys), 2) Dependencies (explicitly declare and isolate dependencies, don't rely on system packages), 3) Config (store config in environment variables, not in code), 4) Backing Services (treat backing services like databases as attached resources, swappable via config), 5) Build/Release/Run (strictly separate build, release, and run stages), 6) Processes (execute as stateless processes, share nothing), 7) Port Binding (export services via port binding, be self-contained), 8) Concurrency (scale out via process model, not threads), 9) Disposability (maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown), 10) Dev/Prod Parity (keep dev, staging, and production as similar as possible), 11) Logs (treat logs as event streams to stdout), 12) Admin Processes (run admin tasks as one-off processes).

Understanding latency numbers every engineer should know (approximations): L1 cache reference 0.5ns, Branch misprediction 5ns, L2 cache reference 7ns, Mutex lock/unlock 25ns, Main memory reference 100ns, Compress 1KB with Snappy 3μs, Send 2KB over 1Gbps network 20μs, Read 1MB sequentially from memory 250μs, RTT within same data center 500μs, Read 1MB sequentially from SSD 1ms, HDD seek 10ms, Read 1MB sequentially from HDD 20ms, Send packet CA to Netherlands to CA 150ms. Implications: in-memory is 1000x faster than disk, disk seeks are expensive (minimize them), data center round trips are fast but trans-continental is slow. Use these numbers to back-of-envelope capacity estimates and justify architectural decisions (e.g., why caching matters, why geographic distribution matters for latency).

Back-of-envelope estimation is essential for system design interviews and capacity planning. Key numbers: 1 billion = 10^9, 1 trillion = 10^12. Traffic: daily active users (DAU) * actions per day / 86400 seconds = QPS. Peak QPS ≈ 2-3x average. Storage: bytes per record * number of records. 1 byte per character, 1KB for small records, 1MB for images. Bandwidth: QPS * response size. Scale factors: 1K = 10^3, 1M = 10^6, 1B = 10^9. Example: design Twitter. 100M DAU, 5 tweets/day = 500M tweets/day = ~6000 tweets/sec writes. Each tweet 280 chars = 280 bytes text + metadata ~1KB. 500M tweets/day * 1KB = 500GB/day storage. 300M reads/day * 100 followers = 30B timeline reads = 350K reads/sec. This justifies precomputed timelines, multiple DB shards, and heavy caching.

Time-series databases (TSDBs) are optimized for storing and querying data indexed by time. Characteristics of time-series data: high write throughput (millions of data points per second), data arrives in time order, queries are mostly time-range based, recent data is hot and older data is cold, and downsampling/aggregation is common. TSDBs optimize for: columnar storage (compress similar time-series values efficiently), automatic downsampling (roll up high-resolution data to lower resolution over time), efficient range queries (scan instead of random access), and retention policies (automatically delete old data). Popular TSDBs: InfluxDB (purpose-built TSDB, InfluxQL and Flux query languages), TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL extension with time-series optimizations), Prometheus (pull-based metrics TSDB), Victoria Metrics (high-performance, resource-efficient), and Apache Cassandra (wide-column store, good for time-series with partition key = time bucket).

Graph databases store data as nodes (entities) and edges (relationships) with properties on both. Optimized for traversal queries that explore relationships, where SQL joins become prohibitively expensive for many-hop queries. Use cases: social networks (mutual friends, friend-of-friend), recommendation engines (who bought this also bought), fraud detection (rings of connected fraudulent accounts), knowledge graphs, supply chain management, and access control systems (checking if user has permission via role/group graph). Query languages: Cypher (Neo4j), Gremlin (Apache TinkerPop, supported by AWS Neptune, JanusGraph), SPARQL (RDF/semantic web). Index-free adjacency: in native graph DBs, each node directly stores pointers to adjacent nodes, enabling O(1) relationship traversal regardless of graph size. This differs from SQL JOIN which scans indexes on both sides.

Vector databases store and query high-dimensional vector embeddings used in machine learning and AI applications. Embeddings are dense numerical representations of data (text, images, audio) generated by ML models where semantically similar items have similar vectors (close in vector space). Core operation: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search finds the k vectors closest to a query vector. ANN algorithms: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World - graph-based, excellent recall-speed trade-off), IVF (Inverted File Index with product quantization for compression), FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search library, open-source). Popular vector databases: Chroma (lightweight, local or hosted, uses HNSW), Pinecone (managed cloud, enterprise-grade), Weaviate (open-source, hybrid search combining vector and keyword), Milvus (open-source, Kubernetes-native, high scale), pgvector (PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity). Use cases: semantic search, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), recommendation systems, image similarity, and anomaly detection.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) augments LLM responses with relevant context retrieved from an external knowledge base. Architecture: Indexing pipeline (ingest documents, split into chunks, generate embeddings for each chunk using an embedding model, store embeddings with metadata in a vector database). Query pipeline (embed the user's query using the same embedding model, perform ANN search in vector DB to find top-k relevant chunks, inject retrieved chunks into the LLM prompt as context, generate response grounded in retrieved context). Chunking strategies: fixed-size (split by character count with overlap), sentence-based (split on sentence boundaries), semantic chunking (split based on topic similarity), and hierarchical (small chunks for retrieval, larger parent chunks for context). Chunking parameters: chunk size (256-1024 tokens typical), overlap (10-20% of chunk size to preserve context at boundaries). Retrieval improvements: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings), multi-query retrieval, re-ranking with cross-encoders.

Embedding models convert text into dense vector representations where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity. Key properties: same embedding model must be used for indexing and query time. Embedding dimensions: smaller (384d, all-MiniLM-L6-v2) are faster and smaller; larger (1536d, text-embedding-ada-002; 3072d, text-embedding-3-large) capture more nuance. Similarity metrics: cosine similarity (angle between vectors, most common for semantic search), dot product (faster, effective when vectors are normalized), and Euclidean distance (L2 distance, less common). Open-source embedding models: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (22MB, fast, good quality, default for ChromaDB), nomic-embed-text (Ollama, runs locally), BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 (larger, higher quality). Commercial: text-embedding-ada-002 (OpenAI, 1536d), text-embedding-3-small (cheaper, newer), Titan Embeddings (Amazon Bedrock). Bi-encoder embeddings (fast retrieval) vs cross-encoders (accurate re-ranking of retrieved results).

ChromaDB is a lightweight, open-source vector database for embedding storage and retrieval, ideal for local development and smaller-scale production. Installation: pip install chromadb. Modes: in-memory (ephemeral), persistent (on-disk with DuckDB+Parquet), and client-server (HTTP API). Core concepts: Client (connects to Chroma instance), Collection (named group of embeddings with metadata, analogous to a table), Documents (text content), Embeddings (vectors), IDs (unique string identifiers), and Metadata (JSON dict for filtering). Default embedding function: uses sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (downloads ~100MB on first run, fully local and free). Operations: collection.add(documents=[], ids=[], metadatas=[]) to index; collection.query(query_texts=[], n_results=k) for retrieval. Metadata filtering: collection.query(where={'topic': 'caching'}) for hybrid search combining vector similarity with metadata filters. Persistence: PersistentClient(path='./chroma_db') saves to disk; embeddings reloaded on next startup without re-indexing.

Designing a web crawler at Google Search scale. Components: URL Frontier (priority queue of URLs to crawl, partitioned by domain to respect crawl-delay), DNS Resolver Cache (cache domain-to-IP mappings to reduce DNS overhead at high QPS), Fetcher (downloads HTML, respects robots.txt, handles redirects), Parser (extracts links and content from HTML), Content Deduplication (SimHash fingerprint to detect near-duplicate pages, Bloom filter for URL deduplication), Content Store (stores raw HTML and extracted text, usually distributed object storage), and Indexer (processes content for search index). Politeness: respect robots.txt exclusion rules, per-domain crawl rate limiting (no more than 1 req/sec per domain), and identify with a User-Agent header. Scale: crawl 1 billion pages requires distributed crawling across hundreds of fetchers partitioned by domain hash. BFS vs DFS: BFS preferred (explores the web broadly, discovers high-quality pages faster).

Designing a payment processing system. Core requirements: exactly-once processing (a payment must be processed exactly once, never twice), idempotency (retrying a failed payment request must not double-charge), atomicity (debit and credit must succeed or both fail), auditability (complete immutable log of all transactions), and compliance (PCI DSS for card data, SOX for financial reporting). Idempotency key: client generates a unique key per payment request; server stores (idempotency_key, response) in DB; on retry, returns stored response without re-processing. Saga for distributed transactions: payment initiation, fraud check, balance deduction, payment provider call, reconciliation. Payment state machine: PENDING -> PROCESSING -> COMPLETED/FAILED/REFUNDED. Ledger: double-entry accounting (every transaction has a debit and credit entry summing to zero). External payment providers: Stripe, Adyen, PayPal (never build payment card processing from scratch). Reconciliation: daily batch job compares internal ledger with payment provider statements.

Designing a video streaming platform like YouTube/Netflix. Upload pipeline: user uploads video, stored in raw object storage (S3), transcoding job queued (Kafka), transcoding workers (EC2 with GPU) convert to multiple resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) and formats (H.264, H.265/HEVC, VP9, AV1) in ABR (Adaptive Bitrate) format (HLS segments or MPEG-DASH chunks). Each segment is 2-10 seconds long. Thumbnails generated from keyframes. Metadata stored in DB. CDN distribution: video segments pushed to CDN edge nodes worldwide. Playback: client starts with lowest quality segment, player monitors bandwidth and switches quality tier per segment (ABR algorithm). Playback URL signed with short-lived token to prevent unauthorized access. Storage: long-tail content on cheaper cold storage (S3 Glacier), hot content on warm storage replicated to CDN. Content metadata: Elasticsearch for full-text search, MySQL for structured metadata. View counting: HyperLogLog for unique viewers, streaming counters in Redis.

Designing a hotel reservation system like Booking.com. Core challenges: concurrency (two users booking the same room simultaneously), inventory management (accurate room availability), and double-booking prevention. Data model: Hotel, RoomType, Room, Reservation (user_id, room_id, check_in, check_out, status), RoomAvailability (room_id, date, is_available). Availability check and booking must be atomic: use SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock room rows during the booking transaction, preventing concurrent bookings. Alternatively, use optimistic locking with a version column. Idempotency: each booking request has an idempotency key. Search: Elasticsearch indexes hotels by location (geo_point), amenities, rating, and price. Availability queries: for a date range, find rooms where no conflicting reservation exists. Cache availability for popular date ranges in Redis. Overbooking prevention: database constraint (unique index on room_id + date range) as the last line of defense. Payment: charge credit card only after reservation confirmed to avoid charging for unavailable rooms.

Designing a stock trading and order matching system. Components: Order Gateway (receives and validates orders from clients), Order Book (maintains sorted lists of buy and sell orders per symbol, matching engine runs here), Matching Engine (matches buy/sell orders by price-time priority - highest buy meets lowest sell; if prices cross, a trade is executed), Trade Engine (executes matched trades, updates positions), Market Data Service (distributes real-time price/trade data to subscribers), Risk Engine (pre-trade risk checks: buying power, position limits, pattern day trader rules), and Settlement Service (T+2 settlement of trades to custodian). Matching engine: in-memory order book sorted by price (BST or sorted arrays) and time. Low latency requirements: matching engines use kernel bypass networking (DPDK), memory-mapped files, and lock-free data structures. Event sourcing: every order state change stored as immutable events for auditability and replay. FIX protocol (Financial Information eXchange) for order communication.

Systematic approach to capacity planning. Step 1 - Traffic estimation: identify DAU, actions per user per day, peak multiplier (2-5x average). Calculate read and write QPS separately. Step 2 - Storage estimation: data size per entity * entity count * replication factor * retention period. Include blob storage (images, videos) separately. Step 3 - Bandwidth estimation: QPS * average response size = outbound bandwidth. Step 4 - Memory estimation: cache ~20% of daily traffic data; 1M cached items at 1KB each = 1GB RAM. Step 5 - Server count: assume 1 web server handles 10K-50K concurrent connections; QPS per server depends on workload type (CPU-bound: hundreds, I/O-bound: thousands). Step 6 - Database server count: read replicas = peak read QPS / queries per DB server; shards = total data / data per shard. Common errors: forgetting replication overhead on write QPS, underestimating storage growth, and ignoring metadata and index overhead (typically 20-50% of data size).

High Availability (HA) targets 99.9% (8.7hr downtime/year), 99.99% (52min), or 99.999% (5min). Achieving HA requires eliminating all single points of failure. Principles: redundancy (multiple instances of every component), geographic distribution (across availability zones and regions), automated failover (detect failures and reroute automatically without human intervention), graceful degradation (core features remain available when non-critical components fail), and health monitoring with automated recovery. Multi-AZ deployments: primary in AZ-a, standby in AZ-b for automated failover (RDS Multi-AZ, Elasticache cluster mode). Multi-region: active-passive (failover only) or active-active (serving traffic from both). Dependency isolation: identify critical vs non-critical dependencies; ensure critical path has no single points of failure. Data replication lag must be accounted for in failover (RPO calculation). DNS TTL: short TTL (60s) enables faster DNS-based failover.

Synchronous communication: direct HTTP/REST or gRPC calls where the caller waits for a response. Simple but creates temporal coupling (both services must be up) and cascading failure risk. Best for: query-response patterns where the result is needed immediately. Asynchronous messaging: producers publish events to a message broker; consumers process independently. Temporal decoupling: producer and consumer don't need to be running simultaneously. Best for: commands where immediate response is not needed and events that multiple services may react to. Request-reply over messaging: publish a command with a correlation_id and reply_to queue; consumer processes and publishes response to reply_to queue. Useful for async request-response without direct coupling. Service choreography vs orchestration: choreography uses events (decentralized, each service reacts to events), orchestration uses a central coordinator (easier to reason about complex flows). Anti-pattern: synchronous chains of 5+ services (amplifies latency and failure probability multiplicatively).

Core AWS services for system design: Compute: EC2 (VMs), Lambda (serverless functions), ECS/EKS (container orchestration), Elastic Beanstalk (managed app deployment). Storage: S3 (object storage, 99.999999999% durability), EBS (block storage for EC2), EFS (shared NFS file system), Glacier (archival storage). Databases: RDS (managed relational: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle), Aurora (cloud-native MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible, 5x faster), DynamoDB (managed NoSQL key-value/document, single-digit ms latency at any scale), ElastiCache (managed Redis/Memcached), Redshift (managed data warehouse), DocumentDB (MongoDB compatible). Networking: VPC (isolated network), CloudFront (CDN), Route 53 (DNS), API Gateway (REST/HTTP/WebSocket API management), ELB (ALB for L7, NLB for L4). Messaging: SQS (managed queue), SNS (pub/sub), Kinesis (real-time streaming), EventBridge (event bus). Identity: IAM (identity and access management), Cognito (user authentication for apps).

topic: Cloud Architecture - Multi-Cloud and Hybrid Cloud
content: Multi-cloud uses services from two or more cloud providers (AWS + GCP + Azure) to avoid vendor lock-in, optimize costs, leverage best-of-breed services, and meet regulatory requirements (data sovereignty). Challenges: increased operational complexity, different APIs and services to manage, data transfer costs between clouds, and latency of cross-cloud communication. Hybrid cloud combines on-premise infrastructure with public cloud, connected via VPN or dedicated links (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute). Use cases: extending on-premise capacity with cloud burst, keeping sensitive data on-premise while using cloud for processing, and gradual cloud migration. Cloud-agnostic architecture: use Kubernetes for portability, Terraform for IaC across providers, and abstract cloud-specific services behind interfaces. Data gravity: large datasets are expensive to move; services tend to gravitate toward where the data lives, creating implicit vendor lock-in even without service-level lock-in.

API versioning manages breaking changes while maintaining backward compatibility for existing clients.
