Strategies: URI versioning (e.g., /v1/users, /v2/users; most visible, easy to test in browser, breaks caching if version changes frequently), Query parameter versioning (/users?version=1; less RESTful, easy to ignore), Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v1+json; clean URIs, harder to test manually), Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (Pact framework; consumers define expected API contract, provider verified against all consumer contracts before deployment - prevents breaking changes). Semantic versioning for APIs: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; major version for breaking changes, minor for additive changes, patch for bug fixes. Deprecation: announce deprecation timeline (minimum 6 months), add Deprecation and Sunset headers, monitor usage of deprecated versions before removal. Never break existing API contracts without incrementing major version.

Idempotency means performing the same operation multiple times produces the same result as doing it once. Critical for reliability in distributed systems where network failures require retries. Implementing idempotency: idempotency key (client generates a unique key per logical operation, typically UUID; server stores processed key with response in a DB/cache; on retry with same key, return stored response without re-processing), natural idempotency (HTTP GET is naturally idempotent; PUT with full resource state is idempotent; DELETE is effectively idempotent), and conditional requests (ETags and If-Match headers detect concurrent modifications). Idempotency key TTL: store keys long enough to cover all retry windows (24-72 hours typical). Payment systems: store idempotency key with payment result; retry of a failed payment with same key returns the original outcome. Database upsert (INSERT ON CONFLICT UPDATE) is idempotent. Event consumers must be idempotent (process each event at-least-once; track processed event IDs to skip duplicates).

Consistency models define how and when writes become visible to readers in a distributed system. Strong consistency (linearizability): every read reflects the most recent write; globally ordered operations; highest correctness but highest latency. Sequential consistency: operations appear in some total order consistent with each process's program order; no real-time guarantee. Causal consistency: causally related operations appear in order (A happened before B is preserved); concurrent operations may be seen in different orders. Eventual consistency: all replicas converge to the same value given no new updates; no timing guarantee; used in highly available systems (DNS, shopping carts). Read-your-writes consistency: after a write, the same client always sees that write in subsequent reads; achieved by routing reads to the primary or using sticky sessions. Monotonic reads: once a client reads a value, subsequent reads will return the same or newer values; prevent 'going back in time'. Session guarantees combine multiple models for practical use.

Database per service pattern: each microservice owns its database; no other service can access it directly. Ensures loose coupling and allows independent schema evolution and technology choice. Shared database anti-pattern: multiple services sharing one DB creates tight coupling (one service's schema change breaks others) and a shared bottleneck. Data composition: when a query spans multiple services, use the API composition pattern (orchestrate calls to multiple services and merge results in the API layer) or the CQRS read model (maintain a denormalized read-side view updated by events from multiple services). Sagas for distributed transactions (see Saga pattern). Dual writes problem: writing to DB and message broker in one operation is not atomic; use the Outbox pattern. Data ownership boundaries: if two services frequently need the same data, consider whether they should be one service or replicate data via events.

An inverted index is the core data structure of a text search engine, mapping terms to the documents containing them. Structure: for each term in the corpus, store a posting list (list of document IDs containing the term, optionally with position and frequency). Indexing pipeline: tokenization (split text into tokens), normalization (lowercase, stemming/lemmatization, stop word removal), posting list construction. Query processing: AND queries intersect posting lists (use smallest first), OR queries union posting lists, NOT queries exclude, phrase queries use positional information to verify term adjacency, and TF-IDF or BM25 scores rank results by relevance. Distributed search (Elasticsearch): index split into shards (each shard is an independent Lucene index); query fan-out to all shards, results merged and scored globally. Segment merging: Lucene writes new segments for each indexing batch; segments periodically merged to reduce search overhead. Near real-time search: segments written to OS cache first (available for search), then flushed to disk (durability).

Geospatial indexing enables efficient proximity search (find restaurants within 5km). Approaches: Geohash (encode latitude/longitude as a string; nearby locations share a prefix; query by expanding prefix radius), S2 Geometry (Google library; hierarchical grid cells at multiple levels of precision; cells are quadrilateral regions; efficient for complex polygon queries and range operations), H3 (Uber's hexagonal hierarchical grid; hexagons have equal-area property and consistent neighbor distance; used for demand heatmaps), and R-tree (spatial index for rectangular bounding boxes; used in PostGIS and SpatiaLite). PostGIS: PostgreSQL extension with ST_DWithin for proximity search, ST_Intersects for polygon containment, and geography type for accurate Earth-surface distance calculation using spherical model. Uber's location platform: driver locations stored in Redis GEOADD, queried with GEORADIUS, partitioned by city for horizontal scaling. Caching tile-based map data at multiple zoom levels in object storage.

topic: Machine Learning System Design - Feature Store
content: A feature store is a centralized repository for computing, storing, and serving ML features to ensure consistency between model training and online inference. Problem: features computed differently in batch training vs real-time serving lead to training-serving skew and degraded model performance. Feature store components: offline store (historical features for training, stored in data warehouse or object storage), online store (low-latency feature serving for inference, stored in Redis or DynamoDB), feature computation (batch jobs or streaming pipelines compute and update features), feature registry (metadata catalog of all features with documentation, lineage, and ownership). Feast (open-source), Tecton, Hopsworks, and AWS Feature Store are popular implementations. Time-travel queries: retrieve feature values as they existed at a specific point in time for point-in-time correct training datasets (prevent feature leakage). Feature sharing: one team's features reusable by others without recomputation.

Serverless computing abstracts infrastructure management; developers deploy code (functions) that execute in response to events. The provider automatically scales, manages servers, and charges per execution. AWS Lambda: functions execute up to 15 minutes, scale from 0 to thousands of concurrent executions in seconds, priced per invocation and duration. Cold start problem: first invocation of a function requires container provisioning (100ms-10s depending on runtime and package size). Mitigations: provisioned concurrency (pre-warm instances), minimize package size, choose faster runtimes (Node.js, Python vs Java). Event sources: API Gateway, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB Streams, S3 events, Kinesis, EventBridge. Serverless patterns: fan-out (one event triggers multiple parallel functions), pipeline (chain of functions via queues), and scatter-gather (parallel functions merge results). Limitations: execution time limit, cold starts, vendor lock-in, difficult to test locally, and stateless (state must be external). Best for: event-driven, variable traffic, short-lived compute.

Blockchain is a distributed ledger where transactions are recorded in cryptographically linked blocks. Each block contains: transactions, timestamp, previous block hash (chain linkage), and nonce (for proof-of-work). Properties: immutability (changing one block invalidates all subsequent blocks), decentralization (no single authority), and transparency (all transactions publicly verifiable). Consensus mechanisms: Proof of Work (miners compete to solve a hash puzzle; energy-intensive; Bitcoin, pre-merge Ethereum), Proof of Stake (validators selected based on staked tokens; energy-efficient; Ethereum post-merge, Cardano), and Delegated Proof of Stake (token holders vote for delegates who validate). Smart contracts: self-executing code deployed on the blockchain triggered by transactions (Ethereum's Solidity, EVM). Permissioned blockchains (Hyperledger Fabric): for enterprise use, known participants, faster consensus (PBFT). Use cases for system design: supply chain traceability, cross-border payments, digital identity, NFTs, and DeFi protocols.

Privacy engineering integrates data protection into system design from the start (Privacy by Design). GDPR key requirements: lawful basis for processing personal data, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure/right to be forgotten, portability, restriction), data minimization (collect only what's necessary), purpose limitation (use data only for stated purpose), storage limitation (don't retain longer than necessary), security (appropriate technical measures), and breach notification (72 hours to authority). Technical implementations: data classification (identify and tag PII), encryption at rest and in transit, access controls and audit logging, data retention automation (auto-delete after retention period), right to erasure (delete or anonymize records on request; challenge with backups - use logical deletion + backup rotation), consent management platforms (CMP) for cookie consent, pseudonymization (replace PII with tokens, store mapping separately), and data residency controls (ensuring EU data stays in EU).

API security must be designed from the ground up. Authentication: always use HTTPS (TLS 1.2+), use OAuth 2.0 with short-lived access tokens (15-60 minutes) and refresh tokens, validate JWT signatures and expiry on every request, and implement MFA for sensitive operations. Authorization: enforce least privilege, validate authorization on every endpoint (not just at gateway), use RBAC or ABAC, and test with negative cases (can user A access user B's data?). Input validation: validate all input types, lengths, and formats; reject unexpected fields; use allowlists not denylists; prevent SQL injection (parameterized queries), XSS (output encoding), and SSRF (validate URLs against allowlist). Rate limiting: per-user and per-IP rate limiting on all endpoints, especially auth endpoints. Secrets management: never log secrets, rotate API keys regularly, use Vault or AWS Secrets Manager. CORS: restrict allowed origins to known domains. Security headers: HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options.

Testing pyramid for distributed systems: Unit tests (fastest, test individual functions in isolation with mocked dependencies), Integration tests (test interactions between a service and its real dependencies like DB, cache; use Docker Compose to spin up dependencies), Component tests (test a single service end-to-end via its API with real infrastructure but mocked external services), Contract tests (Pact: verify producer and consumer agree on API contract without end-to-end tests), End-to-End tests (test full system flows; slow, brittle, expensive; reserve for critical user journeys), and Performance tests (JMeter, Gatling, k6: load testing, stress testing, soak testing). Chaos testing: inject failures in production-like environments. Test data management: use factories/fixtures for realistic test data, ensure test isolation (tests don't share data), and anonymize production data for staging. Mock vs stub vs fake: mocks verify interactions, stubs return canned responses, fakes have working implementations (in-memory DB).

Designing real-time collaborative editing (Google Docs model). Challenge: multiple users simultaneously editing the same document; changes must be merged without conflict and all users must converge to the same state. Approaches: Operational Transformation (OT, used by Google Docs): operations transformed against concurrent operations to maintain causal consistency. Server serializes all operations; clients send operations to server which applies OT and broadcasts. Requires central server. CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, used by Figma, Notion): data structures where concurrent edits automatically merge without conflict. RGA (Replicated Growable Array) for text. No central coordination needed; works peer-to-peer or offline-first. Presence: track which users are viewing or editing (cursor positions, active users list) via WebSocket broadcast. Persistence: store document as event log (event sourcing) to support history and undo. Snapshots: periodic full document state snapshots to limit event log replay length.

Edge computing processes data closer to where it is generated (IoT devices, end users) rather than in centralized cloud data centers. Reduces latency (critical for autonomous vehicles, AR/VR, industrial IoT), reduces bandwidth (process and filter data locally, send only results to cloud), improves privacy (sensitive data processed locally), and enables offline operation. Edge tiers: device edge (processing on the IoT device itself), local edge (on-premise edge servers/gateways in factories, hospitals), and regional edge (CDN PoPs, telco edge nodes). Challenges: resource-constrained hardware, remote management and updates, security (physical access to edge devices), heterogeneous environments, and eventual consistency with central cloud. Platforms: AWS Greengrass (Lambda functions on edge devices), Azure IoT Edge, Cloudflare Workers (serverless at CDN edge), and Fastly Compute@Edge. ML at the edge: TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime for model inference on constrained hardware.

topic: API Rate Limiting and Throttling Design
content: Comprehensive rate limiting strategy: multi-tier limits (per-second burst limit, per-minute sustained limit, per-day quota), per-resource limits (e.g., search endpoint has stricter limits than profile reads), and tier-based limits (free: 100 req/min, pro: 1000 req/min, enterprise: 10000 req/min). Implementation layers: edge/CDN rate limiting (Cloudflare rate limiting for DDoS protection), API gateway rate limiting (Kong, AWS API Gateway throttling), and application-level rate limiting (Redis-based, most flexible). Graceful limiting: return 429 with Retry-After header, clear error message, and upgrade CTA. Distributed rate limiting: Redis Cluster with Lua scripts for atomic counter operations; use Redis INCR + EXPIRE for fixed window or sorted sets for sliding window. Rate limit bypass prevention: limit by user ID (for authenticated requests) and by IP (for unauthenticated), use device fingerprinting for additional identity signals, and apply stricter limits to suspicious patterns.

Data modeling principles for scalable systems. Normalization (OLTP workloads): eliminate redundancy by decomposing into related tables (1NF, 2NF, 3NF). Reduces storage and update anomalies but increases JOIN complexity. Denormalization (OLAP/read-heavy workloads): combine tables and duplicate data for query performance. Avoids expensive JOINs at the cost of data redundancy and update complexity. Choosing primary keys: use surrogate keys (auto-increment or UUID) rather than natural keys (email, SSN) which may change. UUID as primary key in distributed systems avoids coordination for ID generation. JSON columns: store semi-structured data in JSONB (PostgreSQL) for flexible schemas, with JSON path indexes for performance. Polymorphism patterns: single-table inheritance (all subtypes in one table with type discriminator column), class-table inheritance (base table + subtype tables joined on PK), concrete-table inheritance (separate table per subtype, no sharing). Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV): flexible but slow; avoid unless truly dynamic attributes are needed.

Effective monitoring strategy: USE method for resources (Utilization - % time busy, Saturation - work queue depth, Errors - error rate), RED method for services (Rate - requests per second, Errors - error rate, Duration - latency distribution). Golden signals: latency (p50, p95, p99), traffic (requests/sec), errors (error rate %), and saturation (resource utilization %). Alert philosophy: alert on symptoms (user-facing impact) not causes (disk at 80%); high signal-to-noise ratio (low false positives); actionable alerts (alert only if someone must act now); and page only for urgent issues (PagerDuty for critical, Slack for warnings). SLO-based alerting: burn rate alerts trigger when error budget is being consumed too fast (Google SRE burn rate model: 1-hour window firing when burn rate > 14.4x budget consumption rate). Runbooks: every alert links to a runbook with diagnosis steps and resolution procedures. Post-mortems: blameless post-mortem for every P1 incident, tracking root cause and action items.

Structured approach to system design interviews. Step 1 - Requirements clarification (5 min): ask about functional requirements (what features?), non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability, consistency), scale (DAU, QPS, storage), and constraints. Step 2 - High-level design (10 min): draw major components (clients, load balancers, servers, databases, caches, queues), describe data flow, identify the core entities and key APIs. Step 3 - Deep dive (20 min): focus on the most interesting/challenging components; discuss data model, database choice justification, scaling bottlenecks, and failure handling. Step 4 - Trade-off discussion (5 min): acknowledge what your design sacrifices, alternative approaches, and what you'd improve with more time. Communication tips: think aloud, validate understanding before diving deep, make decisions confidently and explain rationale, handle follow-up questions gracefully, and use concrete numbers from back-of-envelope estimates to justify design choices.
